title: The periodic table
summary: The periodic table is a map of the elements. An element's place tells you how it behaves.
cards.0.p: In 1869 Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements by mass and put similar ones in the same column. He left gaps for elements not yet found and predicted their properties. One of them, gallium, was found in 1875.
cards.0.svg#0: Leave a gap, make a prediction
cards.1.p: In 1913 Moseley showed that the true order of the elements is their atomic number (number of protons). Today's table is arranged this way and holds 118 elements.
cards.1.svg#7: By mass, I should have come first
cards.1.key: Modern periodic table = arranged by atomic number (Z)
cards.1.once.soru: Tellurium (127.6) is heavier than iodine (126.9) but comes before it in the table. What is the modern table arranged by?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: In 1913 Moseley showed that the true order is the number of protons. Te has 52 protons, and I has 53.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: If it were arranged by mass, Te and I would swap places.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The table is arranged by the structure of the atom, not by the order of discovery.
cards.2.p: The horizontal rows of the table are called periods, and there are 7. The period number gives the number of shells. The vertical columns are called groups, and there are 18. Elements in the same main group have similar valence electrons and chemical properties.
cards.2.key: He has 2 valence electrons, but it sits in group 18 (8A).
cards.3.p: On the left and in the middle are the metals (shiny, conductive), at the upper right the nonmetals, between them the metalloids, and at the far right the noble gases. Metallic character increases to the left and down.
cards.3.etk.soru: Put each element in the right group.
cards.3.etk.ogeler.6.2: It sits on the left of the table in 1A, but it is a nonmetal.
cards.4.p: The main group number gives the number of valence electrons, with He as the only exception. Group 1A is called the alkali metals, 2A the alkaline earth metals, 7A the halogens and 8A the noble gases.
cards.4.key: In the 1-18 numbering, the last digit of groups 13-18 gives the A group number.
cards.4.once.soru: Chlorine is in group 7A. How many electrons are in its outer shell?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The main group number gives the number of valence electrons. An element in group 7A has 7 valence electrons.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: Elements in group 1A have 1 valence electron.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: 17 is chlorine's total number of electrons. Its outer shell has 7.
cards.5.p: Going down a group, the number of shells increases, so the atom gets bigger. Going right across a period, the number of protons increases, the nucleus pulls the electrons harder, and the atom gets smaller. A cation is smaller than its atom, and an anion is bigger.
cards.5.key: It increases down a group and decreases to the right. A cation is smaller than its atom, and an anion is bigger than its atom.
cards.6.p: Ionization energy increases to the right across a period and decreases down a group. There are two exceptions. Going from Be to B and from N to O, the ionization energy drops, because the s² and half-full p³ configurations are more stable.
cards.6.key: Group 2A has a higher ionization energy than 3A, and 5A higher than 6A. This is because the s² and p³ configurations are spherically symmetric and more stable.
cards.7.p: As electrons are removed one by one, each one takes more energy. When the valence electrons run out and an inner shell is reached, the energy jumps suddenly. The number of electrons before the jump gives the group number.
cards.7.svg#13: IE₂ → IE₃: jumps more than 5 times
cards.7.key: The number of electrons before the big jump equals the number of valence electrons and the main group number.
cards.7.once.soru: An atom's successive ionization energies are 738, 1451 and 7733 kJ/mol. How many valence electrons does it have?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The first two electrons come off the outer shell easily. The third comes from an inner shell, so the energy jumps. This element, with 2 valence electrons, is magnesium in group 2A.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The third electron comes from an inner shell. So it is not a valence electron.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: The second electron also comes off easily. The big jump comes after it.
cards.8.p: Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls the shared electrons in a bond toward itself. It increases to the right and decreases going down. Fluorine is the most electronegative, and oxygen is second.
cards.8.svg#15: Down the group: F 4.0 · Cl 3.2 · Br 3.0 · I 2.7
cards.8.key: Electronegativity increases to the right and up. Fluorine has the highest electronegativity.
cards.8.once.soru: In the H–F bond, which atom are the shared electrons closer to?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and it pulls the electrons in the bond toward itself.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Hydrogen pulls much more weakly than fluorine.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Equal sharing happens only between two identical atoms, as in H–H.
cards.9.p: The energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron is its electron affinity. The highest values are found in the halogens. Nonmetallic character increases to the right and up.
cards.9.key: The highest electron affinity belongs to chlorine, not fluorine. In the small F atom, the electrons repel each other.
cards.9.once.soru: Atoms of which group are most eager to gain electrons?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: When halogens gain one electron, they reach a noble gas configuration. So their electron affinities are the highest.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: These are eager to give up electrons, not to gain them.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Noble gases already have a stable configuration. So they are not eager to gain electrons.
cards.10.h: s, p, d and f blocks
cards.10.p: The subshell that the last electron enters sets the element's block. 1A, 2A and He are in the s block, and groups 3A–8A are in the p block. The B groups form the d block, and they are called transition metals. The lanthanides and actinides are in the f block.
cards.10.svg#6: He (1s²) is in the s block but sits in 8A.
cards.10.key: The main groups (A groups) are made of the s and p blocks. The transition metals (B groups) are in the d block.
cards.10.once.soru: Iron (Fe) is in the B groups in the middle of the table. Which subshell does its last electron enter?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶, and the last electron enters 3d. The B groups in the middle of the table are the d block.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Elements ending in s are the two groups at the far left of the table.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Elements ending in p are the six groups on the right of the table.
cards.11.p:
• The modern table is arranged by atomic number and has 7 periods and 18 groups.
• The period number gives the number of shells, and the main group number gives the number of valence electrons.
• Metals are on the left, nonmetals at the upper right and noble gases at the far right.
• Toward the upper right, the radius decreases, and ionization energy and electronegativity usually increase.
cards.11.svg#0: ↗ toward upper right: IE and electronegativity increase
cards.11.svg#1: ↙ toward lower left: atomic radius increases
quiz.0.q: Order these from highest to lowest electronegativity. (F: period 2, 7A; Cl: period 3, 7A; S: period 3, 6A; Na: period 3, 1A)
quiz.0.e: Electronegativity increases to the right and up. F is at the upper right (4.0). Cl is below it (3.2), S is to the left of Cl (2.6), and Na is at the far left of the period (0.9).
quiz.1.q: Order these isoelectronic ions from largest to smallest radius. (Z: S 16, Cl 17, K 19, Ca 20)
quiz.1.e: All four particles have 18 electrons. As the number of protons grows, the nucleus pulls the same electrons harder. So S²⁻ with 16 protons is the largest, and Ca²⁺ with 20 protons is the smallest.
quiz.2.q: A main-group atom has these successive ionization energies (kJ/mol): IE₁ = 578, IE₂ = 1817, IE₃ = 2745, IE₄ = 11 577. How many valence electrons does it have?
quiz.2.e: The big jump comes from IE₃ to IE₄ (2745 → 11 577). So the first 3 electrons are valence electrons, and the fourth comes from an inner shell. The atom is in group 3A, and it is aluminum.
quiz.3.q: Which one has the greatest metallic character? (Na: period 3, 1A; K: period 4, 1A; Mg: period 3, 2A; Al: period 3, 3A)
quiz.3.e: Metallic character increases to the left and down. K is both at the far left (1A) and below Na. Its valence electron is farthest from the nucleus, so it comes off most easily.
quiz.3.y.0: Na is also in group 1A, but K is below it. Going down, the electron comes off more easily.
quiz.3.y.2: Mg is to the right of Na. Metallic character decreases to the right.
quiz.3.y.3: Al is the farthest right of these three in period 3. So its metallic character is the smallest.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Fill the gap Mendeleev left, find an element and grow the atoms.
A:adimlar.0.metin: No known element fit between silicon and tin. So Mendeleev left a gap there.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What should the element in the gap be like?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In the column, mass increases from top to bottom. The gap is between silicon and tin.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Mendeleev put an element with a mass of about 72, similar to silicon, in the gap. In 1886 germanium was found, with a mass of 72.6. The prediction held, and the table gained trust.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Mendeleev left the gap for an element that had not been found yet.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The period (row) number gives the number of shells, and the A group number gives the number of electrons in the outer shell. Find the 7A element in period 3.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: This element has 3 shells, with 7 electrons in the outer one. So its electrons are arranged 2-8-7.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: This element is chlorine, with electrons arranged 2-8-7. It has three shells, so it is in period 3. It has 7 electrons in its outer shell, so it is in group 7A. In the 1-18 numbering, it is in group 17.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Oxygen is selected. Change the atomic number and look at its neighbors.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Which element is chemically most like oxygen?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Nitrogen is oxygen's neighbor, but it is in group 5A. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons, and oxygen has 6.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Fluorine is in the same period, but in group 7A. Look for similarity in the group, not the period.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Sulfur (2-8-6), like oxygen (2-6), is in group 6A, and both have 6 valence electrons. Both tend to gain two electrons and form −2 ions.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Elements are grouped as metals, nonmetals, metalloids and noble gases. These groups gather in certain regions of the table.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: Where in the table are the elements that are shiny, conduct electricity and can be drawn into wire?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The upper right belongs to nonmetals such as oxygen and sulfur. Most nonmetals do not conduct electricity.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: On the left and in the middle
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Metals are on the left and in the middle of the table. Nonmetals are at the upper right, metalloids such as silicon on the border, and noble gases at the far right.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The far right column is the noble gases. They hardly react at all.
A:adimlar.4.metin: The circles show the size of the atoms. Find the largest atom among the first 20 elements.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: Go down to the period with the most shells, then to the far left of that period.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The largest atom is potassium (K). It has 4 shells and sits at the far left of its period. The largest atoms are at the lower left, and the smallest at the upper right.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The energy needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom is called its ionization energy. We will plot the values for the first 20 elements.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: The atoms that give up an electron most easily, with the lowest ionization energy, are in which group?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Quite the opposite: noble gases have the highest value in each period. Removing an electron from their full outer shell is very hard.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Halogens have high ionization energies. They tend to gain electrons rather than give them up.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Li, Na and K have the lowest values in each period, because their single valence electron comes off easily. The value usually rises to the right across a period and falls down a group.
A:kapanis.0: The modern table is arranged by atomic number and has 7 periods and 18 groups.
A:kapanis.1: The period number gives the number of shells, and the main group number gives the number of valence electrons. Elements in the same group behave alike.
A:kapanis.2: Metals are on the left and in the middle, nonmetals at the upper right, metalloids on the border and noble gases at the far right.
A:kapanis.3: Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases to the right across a period.
A:kapanis.4: Ionization energy and electronegativity usually increase to the right and up. The most electronegative element is fluorine.
